summary: This document specifies extensions and procedures to establish dynamic multi-segment pseudowires along explicit paths. This allows diverse primary and backup paths for protection, or controlled signaling for special pseudowires.

eli5.summary: If you want a trip to go through certain cities, you write the route down. This RFC lets network operators write down the exact route for a virtual wire.

questions: what is an explicit route tlv
how to set up diverse backup pseudowire path
subtitle: How a pseudowire can be told exactly which switching routers to cross, using LDP explicit route hops.

tldr.problem: Dynamic multi-segment pseudowires pick their own path, but operators sometimes need diverse primary and backup paths for 1:1 protection, or controlled strict or loose signaling.
tldr.mechanism: The Label Mapping message carries an Explicit Route TLV listing hops, and the RFC adds a new ER-Hop type, L2 PW Address of Switching Point (0x0805), plus rules for how each node consumes the list.
tldr.outcome: A source terminating PE can set up an MS-PW along an explicit path through chosen S-PEs, with defined error codes when the path cannot be followed.

today: RFC 7392 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2014. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Explicit Paths for MS-PWs
sections.content:
Dynamic Multi-Segment Pseudowires (MS-PWs) normally have their paths chosen automatically by a dynamic routing protocol, as defined in RFC 7267. For 1:1 protection with primary and backup MS-PWs, the two must go through diverse sets of Switching Provider Edges (S-PEs) so that no single point of failure exists at the PW level. RFC 7267 allows this using BGP-based mechanisms.

This RFC adds another way: the Source Terminating PE (ST-PE) can choose explicitly which S-PEs the pseudowire passes through. Explicit routing may also be needed for controlled setup and network resource management.

The RFC notes that in many deployments the ST-PE has no view of the S-PE topology, so the route has to come from a management application. How that application works out the route is outside the scope.
sections.eli5: Usually the network picks the road by itself. Sometimes you want a second road that shares no stops with the first, so one closed road cannot ruin both trips.

sections.title: Explicit Route TLVs and Abstract Nodes
sections.content:
The extension is made to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). An explicitly routed MS-PW is set up with a Label Mapping message that carries an ordered list of the S-PEs it should cross. The list is encoded as a series of Explicit Route Hop TLVs (ER-Hop TLVs) inside one Explicit Route TLV (ER-TLV). Both formats come from Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of RFC 3212.

Each hop names an abstract node: a group of one or more S-PEs identified by an IPv4, IPv6 or S-PE address. Each S-PE MUST have an address assigned as in Section 3.2 of RFC 7267, and an S-PE without one that receives a dynamic MS-PW Label Mapping MUST follow the RFC 7267 procedures.

RFC 3212 already defines four ER-Hop types: IPv4 Prefix, IPv6 Prefix, Autonomous System Number and LSP-ID. The semantics of the IPv4 and IPv6 types are left as in RFC 3212.
sections.eli5: Each stop on the list is a 'place', and a place can be a single town or a small group of towns. The list tells the trip the order of places to pass.

sections.title: The L2 PW Address ER-Hop
sections.content:
The new ER-Hop type is L2 PW Address of Switching Point, value 0x0805. It carries an L2 PW Address taken from the Generalized PWid FEC AII Type 2 structure of RFC 5003.

The TLV has a U and an F bit, which MUST be zero, with the procedures of RFC 5036 followed when the TLV is not known; a 14-bit Type; and a Length of 18. The L bit is set for a loose hop and cleared for a strict hop. Reserved bits are zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. PreLen is a prefix length from 1 to 96, covering the Global ID, Prefix and AC ID fields. The remaining fields (AII Type, Length, Global ID, Prefix and AC ID) are set and read as in Section 3.2 of RFC 5003.
sections.eli5: The new kind of stop on the list is described by a special address label, with a flag saying whether the trip must go exactly there or may take detours to get there.

sections.title: How Nodes Process the Route
sections.content:
A node that receives a Label Mapping message with an ER-TLV evaluates the first ER-Hop. If the L bit is not set and the node is not inside the abstract node, the node MUST reply with a Label Release carrying the status code "Bad Initial ER-Hop Error" (0x04000004). If the L bit is set, the node picks a next hop along the path to that abstract node. A message with an ER-TLV but no ER-Hop is an error that SHOULD return "Bad Explicit Routing TLV Error" (0x04000001). A Label Mapping with no ER-TLV is processed as in RFC 7267.

Then the node works through the list. If no more hops follow the first, the explicit route has ended and the ER-TLV MUST be removed. If the node is also part of the second hop's abstract node, it deletes the first hop and repeats. If it is adjacent to the second hop's abstract node, it picks a next hop there and deletes the first hop. Otherwise it picks a next hop inside the first abstract node that leads toward the second. If none exists, a strict second hop gives "Bad Strict Node Error" (0x04000002), while a loose second hop lets the node choose any next hop toward it, with "Bad Loose Node Error" (0x04000003) if no path exists in the MPLS domain. Finally the node rewrites the first hop so the next node will accept it, and forwards the message.

Each node MUST find a loop-free path before signaling; RFC 6073 Section 7.6 gives a way to check this. An S-PE that cannot find one MUST release the message with status "PW Loop Detected".
sections.eli5: Every stop checks the list. If it is the right place, it crosses itself off and passes the trip on toward the next place. If it cannot, it sends the trip back with a note saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Adding Hops Along the Way
sections.content: After choosing a next hop, a node MAY change the explicit route. If the ER-TLV was removed because the route ended, the node MAY add a new one. If the node is a member of the first hop's abstract node, it MAY insert a series of hops before the first hop or replace it, and each inserted hop MUST denote an abstract node that is a subset of the current one. If the first hop is loose, an arbitrary series of hops MAY be inserted ahead of it.
sections.eli5: A stop may fill in more detail about its own part of the trip, or, if the stop was loose, add extra stops on the way to it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 5036, RFC 4447 and RFC 7267, which apply to these extensions. As with RFC 7267, automatic path selection means the network chooses the S-PEs that forward packets. Operators can use the VCCV trace mechanisms of RFC 6073 to verify the path actually taken.

IANA assigned a code point from the IETF consensus part of the LDP TLV Type Name Space: 0x0805, L2 PW Address of Switching Point. The Explicit Route TLV, IPv4 Prefix ER-Hop and IPv6 Prefix ER-Hop types were already in the registry.
sections.eli5: The old safety rules still apply, and operators can trace the real route to check it went where it should.

viz.caption: STATUS CODES FOR EXPLICIT ROUTE ERRORS (RFC 7392)

items.label: Bad Explicit Routing TLV Error
items.desc: ER-TLV present but contains no ER-Hop TLV.

items.label: Bad Strict Node Error
items.desc: No path to a strict next hop exists.

items.label: Bad Loose Node Error
items.desc: No path to a loose next hop exists in the MPLS domain.

items.label: Bad Initial ER-Hop Error
items.desc: First hop is strict and the node is not in it.
